name: Bornite (Peacock Ore)
toxicityNote: Contains copper; tarnishes easily and may release copper compounds when damp. Avoid dust, wash hands after handling, do not make elixirs and keep from children and pets.
spiritual: Opens the heart and solar plexus
physical: Traditionally associated with a bright, energized feeling
Kept nearby for comfort during stressful times
Linked by crystal healers to vitality
summary: Bornite, called peacock ore, is a copper iron sulfide that tarnishes to blue, purple and pink iridescence, a stone of joy, happiness and playful balance.
intro: Bornite is the peacock of the mineral world. Freshly broken, it is a bronze-brown to coppery pink, but within hours of air exposure the surface tarnishes into oil-slick blues, purples, magentas and golds. This is the iridescent effect that gives peacock ore its name. Specimens are often sold as rounded nuggets or chunks, usually from Mexico and Chile, sometimes polished into tumbles. It is soft, about 3, and fragile. In the crystal world, bornite is loved as a happy stone, a mineral with an evident sense of fun, that pairs well with bright colored crystals.
history: Bornite was named in 1845 for Ignaz von Born, an Austrian mineralogist. It is an important copper ore, containing about 63 percent copper, and has been mined for centuries. Miners called it variegated copper ore because of its colors. In the nineteenth century it was sometimes carved into small ornaments. The nickname peacock ore is also applied to chalcopyrite with similar tarnish. Its metaphysical meaning as a stone of happiness arose in the twentieth-century crystal movement, inspired by the colorful surface.
meaning: Crystal healers regard bornite as a stone of happiness and emotional lightness. Its shifting colors are linked to the heart and solar plexus, and it is said to lift low moods, encourage delight in small things and release emotional heaviness. Practitioners call it a stone for letting go of old patterns and embracing joy, especially useful during periods of change. Because it is rich in copper, some say it conducts good energy. Emotionally it is associated with playfulness, flexibility and optimism. Traditionally it is also linked to vitality and a warm, bright feeling. Many keep it on a desk for a daily dose of color and cheer.
howToUse: Place a bornite piece on your desk or altar and let its colors catch your eye while you work. Hold it in the palm while recalling a happy memory and breathe slowly. Include a bornite nugget in a joy or happiness grid with citrine and clear quartz. Avoid carrying it loose, since it can scratch and tarnish. Because it is soft and contains copper, keep it as a display piece and wash your hands after handling.
care: Bornite is soft and tarnishes in air and moisture, so keep it dry. Dust with a soft dry brush and avoid acids, perfumes and cleaners. Cleanse with sound, smoke, breath or moonlight. Do not use water, which can dull the colors and cause corrosion. Handle with clean hands, wash afterward and avoid dust. Never use in elixirs. Store in a dry box away from humidity and children.
identify: Genuine bornite is bronze to coppery when fresh and tarnishes quickly to vivid blue, purple and pink. It has a grey-black streak and is soft enough for a knife to scratch. Chalcopyrite is more golden and has greener streak. Many bright rainbow stones sold as peacock ore are actually treated chalcopyrite or heat- and acid-treated pyrite. Titanium-coated quartz is another fake. Natural tarnish is uneven, while coated pieces look uniform.

faq.q: Why is bornite called peacock ore?
faq.a: Bornite develops a vivid tarnish of blue, purple, pink and green that resembles peacock feathers. The same nickname is used for some chalcopyrite, so it is worth checking what mineral you are actually buying.
In crystal tradition bornite is used for joy, happiness and playful balance. People keep it on desks or altars to lift mood and bring a sense of delight into daily life.
